title: Just Say No to... Bottled Water
summary: Josh and Chuck examine bottled water: its history from the 1800s through the 1980s-90s rebranding (Perrier, Orson Welles ad, Pepsi's AquaFina, Coke's Dasani) and its rise to the most-consumed US beverage by 2017. They cover the kinds of bottled water the FDA regulates (artesian, mineral, naturally sparkling, purified, spring, well), FDA versus EPA standards (including lead and bacteria), the voluntary International Bottled Water Association, unregulated intrastate water in some states, labeling misleading claims (Alaska Water, Glacier Clear), taste tests, and the health concerns of plastic leaching and microplastics (2018 Frontiers in Chemistry study). They also discuss single-use plastic recycling problems, corn-based PLA bottles, extended producer responsibility laws, and the Safe Drinking Water Act. The episode closes with a listener mail about the documentary Strad Style.

segments.title: Opening banter and personal anecdote
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode, which draws on an older HowStuffWorks article by Julia Layton, and notes updated consumption statistics (seven billion gallons in 2005 versus fifteen billion gallons by 2019). The hosts joke about bottled water habits and a relative who insists on bottles to track hydration.

segments.title: History of bottled water and its rebranding
segments.summary: Bottled water dates to the 18th and mid-19th centuries, often sold at spas as a remedy. Perrier was rebranded in the 1970s and 80s as a status symbol, with Orson Welles in ads and a People magazine feature. Pepsi launched AquaFina in 1994, Coke followed with Dasani, and brands like Arrowhead and Poland Springs were consolidated by larger companies. Bottled water became the most consumed US beverage in 2017.

segments.title: Tap water versus bottled water and Florida sulfur water
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why people choose bottled over tap water, the disconnect between the two camps, and that tap water is generally safe in most of America, unlike the Flint crisis. Florida's sulfur-heavy 'egg water' is discussed. Reverse osmosis removes beneficial minerals as well as impurities.

segments.title: Misleading bottled water labels
segments.summary: Labels can stretch the truth. Alaska Water sold Juneau municipal tap water as glacier water, and Glacier Clear, owned by Dairy Farmers of America until 2002, was sourced from Greenville, Tennessee. The hosts note that such marketing persisted despite the early 2000s backlash.

segments.title: FDA categories of bottled water
segments.summary: The hosts define the water types the FDA regulates. Artesian water comes from a confined aquifer under pressure. Mineral water has at least 250 ppm of total dissolved solids (the transcript says two parts per million, while spring water has fifty; this is as spoken). Naturally sparkling water must keep its natural carbonation. Josh notes that many brands recarbonate after bottling. Purified water is treated tap or other municipal water by filtering, distillation, reverse osmosis, ozonation, or UV. Spring water is collected from an underground spring, and well water comes from a well.

segments.title: FDA regulation, labeling, fluoride and voluntary industry standards
segments.summary: The FDA regulates bottled water as a packaged food and considers it low risk. Bottled water must state its source type on the label, and sources and additives must be disclosed. Bottled water is typically not fluoridated. The FDA allows more lead and some contaminants than the EPA permits in tap water in some cases, and it allows more bacteria than the EPA does for tap water. State regulation varies, with some states having none. Intrastate-only bottlers can fall outside FDA oversight, and the International Bottled Water Association offers voluntary standards and certification.

segments.title: Plastic leaching and microplastics in bottled water
segments.summary: Heat and long storage can cause plastics such as polycarbonate, PVC and polystyrene, along with phthalates, to leach into water, and reusing bottles may increase leaching. A 2018 Frontiers in Chemistry study of 259 bottles from 11 countries found microplastics in nearly all of them, with an average of 325 particles per liter and as many as 10,000 per liter in one Nestle Pure Life sample. The hosts note polypropylene, a bottle plastic, may be an endocrine disruptor.

segments.title: Single-use plastic waste, recycling and PLA alternatives
segments.summary: Plastic bottle recycling has risen, with the US reportedly recycling a large share, though China's refusal of recyclables created problems. Corn-based PLA bioplastic is compostable but rarely reaches a compost pile and can contaminate recycling. Extended producer responsibility laws in Washington, Maine and Michigan would make producers responsible for packaging waste. The hosts also mention the Great Pacific garbage patch and the Diarrhea Planet band references.

segments.title: Taste, tap water safety and the Safe Drinking Water Act
segments.summary: Blind taste tests often show people cannot tell bottled and tap water apart or rate tap water higher. A celebrity show with a water sommelier is mentioned. The hosts argue that US tap water is generally safe, but the Safe Drinking Water Act has not been updated in about 25 years, and limits are not necessarily scientifically safe. They also mention the documentary Flint: The Poisoning of an American City.

segments.title: Resources and closing remarks on alternatives
segments.summary: The hosts recommend sources including the Environmental Working Group tap water database, Serious Eats, and Time magazine. They joke about box water as a packaging alternative.
topics: Environmental Working Group tap water database

segments.title: Listener mail: documentary Strad Style
segments.summary: A listener, filmmaker Stephen Abalos, promotes his documentary Strad Style about an Ohio man who attempts to copy a famous Stradivarius violin, and the hosts praise the film. The episode ends with the show's sign-off.
